title: Why Laika Really Went to Space
topic: Why the Soviet space program used “dog” Laika on Sputnik 2 in 1957 (to test life‑support systems before sending humans)

lines: A Soviet engineer strapped a trembling dog into a cramped metal can.
Colleagues laughed, saying a stray could never survive a launch.
Khrushchev demanded a “space spectacular” for the October Revolution anniversary.
Korolev had less than four weeks to finish a new satellite.
He grabbed a small dog cage and bolted it onto the rocket.
You see, it’s like testing a car’s seatbelt on a dummy before letting a driver sit behind the wheel.
The real reason: Laika was a living test for the cabin’s air system.
The capsule held an oxygen maker, a filter to soak up bad air, and a fan that turned on when it got too hot.
Scientists watched her breathing, pulse, and temperature from the ground.
The twist? The mission never planned to bring her home.
Laika was a one‑way sacrifice, proving the cabin could keep any creature alive, even if that creature never left orbit.

claims.claim: Khrushchev demanded a space spectacular for the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution, forcing a rushed satellite launch.
Sergei Korolev proposed placing a dog in the satellite to meet the deadline, and the decision was made with less than four weeks to design the craft.
Sputnik 2’s cabin contained an oxygen generator, carbon‑dioxide absorbers, and a fan that activated above 15 °C to keep the passenger alive.
The mission was never designed to retrieve Laika; she was expected to die, serving only to test life‑support systems for future human flights.
